passages.t: Two scouts, and the woman who hid them
passages.happening:
Before Israel crosses, Joshua sends two men ahead in secret. “Go, inspect the land, especially Jericho” (verse 1). They cross the river, enter the city, and lodge in the house of a prostitute named Rahab.

Someone sees them. The king of Jericho hears that men of Israel have come to spy, and he sends to Rahab: “Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house, for they have come to spy out the whole land” (verse 3).

Rahab has already hidden them. She had taken them up to her flat roof and covered them with the stalks of flax she had laid out there (verse 6). To the king's men she says, “Yes, the men did come to me, but I did not know where they had come from. At dusk, when the gate was about to close, the men went out, and I do not know which way they went” (verses 4-5). She tells them to hurry after them.

The king's men set off down the road toward the river crossings, and the city gate is shut behind them (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Jericho was the first city on the far side of the Jordan. It was an oasis fed by a strong spring, and it guarded the road from the river valley up into the hills. Like other towns of Canaan in that age, it had its own king. What archaeologists have found at the site is debated, and the book page sets out the views.

The text says plainly what Rahab was. The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for a prostitute, and the New Testament keeps it (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). Some ancient Jewish interpreters described her as an innkeeper, and some scholars suggest her house served as an inn as well. Either way, it was a house where strangers could come and go without much notice. That is probably why the scouts went there. The book offers no other reason and hints at none.

Flat roofs were places for work and storage. Flax was laid out on them to dry before it was made into linen. The flax harvest in the Jordan valley came in spring, which fits the time of year the book gives for the crossing.

The story is told with suspense and some dry humor. The king's men search the roads while the men they want lie on the roof above them. A king is outwitted by a woman whose trade put her at the edge of her city. And the scouts, who were sent to find things out, do almost nothing. Everything that matters in this chapter is done by Rahab.

She is a Canaanite, living in the first city that stands in Israel's way. The book has barely begun, and the person it shows acting with courage is not an Israelite.
passages.later:
Two New Testament writers remember this night. Hebrews says, “By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient” (Hebrews 11:31). James asks, “In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route?” (James 2:25).

The Bible tells of other women who deceived a king to save lives. When Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill the baby boys, “The midwives, however, feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live” (Exodus 1:17). They gave Pharaoh a misleading answer, and the text says, “So God was good to the midwives” (Exodus 1:20).
passages.hard:
Rahab lied to the king's men. Does the Bible approve of lying?

The chapter reports what she said and makes no comment on it. The New Testament praises her, and it is careful about what it praises. Hebrews names her faith and her welcome of the scouts. James names what she did for them. Neither says that the lie itself was good.

Christians have weighed her lie in two main ways.

Some, following Augustine, hold that lying is always wrong. On this view Rahab is praised for her faith and her kindness in spite of the lie, and not because of it. She was a woman who had only just come to believe in Israel's God and was still learning his ways.

Others hold that to deceive people who are engaged in unjust killing is not the kind of lie the commandment forbids. The commandment reads, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16). They point to the Hebrew midwives, who deceived Pharaoh and were treated well by God. The same question has come up in later times, as when people have hidden those hunted by persecutors and lied to the ones hunting them.

These notes do not choose between the two. Both sides agree on what the story is about. It is about a woman's faith and courage at a moment that could have cost her life, and it is not a general permission to deceive.
passages.asks: Rahab had a few minutes to decide whose side she was on, and it could have killed her. Ask where trusting God has put you at odds with the people around you, or might. Then notice who this woman was. Ask whether there is anyone you have already decided God could not use, because of their past or their trade, and whether you have decided that about yourself.

passages.t: ‘The LORD your God is God in the heavens above’
passages.happening:
Before the scouts sleep, Rahab climbs to the roof and speaks. It is the longest speech in the chapter.

“I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you” (verse 9). She tells them what Jericho has heard: how the LORD dried up the Red Sea when Israel left Egypt, and what Israel did to Sihon and Og, the two kings east of the Jordan (verse 10).

Then she says what she herself has come to believe: “for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below” (verse 11).

And she asks. “Now therefore, please swear to me by the LORD that you will indeed show kindness to my family, because I showed kindness to you” (verse 12). She names them: her father and mother, her brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them (verse 13).

The men answer with an oath. ‘Our lives for your lives’ (verse 14). If she keeps their errand secret, they will deal kindly and faithfully with her when the LORD gives Israel the land.
passages.hearers:
The crossing of the Red Sea lay forty years in the past. The news had traveled the trade roads all that time, and the defeat of Sihon and Og was fresh. Everyone in Jericho had heard the same reports. Rahab says ‘we have heard’ and ‘our hearts melted’. The whole city was afraid.

Fear did not lead the city to do what she did. The king heard the same news and sent men to seize the scouts. Rahab heard it and drew a conclusion about God. Her words in verse 11 are very close to words Moses spoke to Israel: ‘the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below’ (Deuteronomy 4:39). A Canaanite woman who had never stood at Sinai makes Israel's own confession, and she makes it before Israel has done anything in her land.

She uses God's name. English Bibles print ‘the LORD’ in capital letters where the Hebrew has the personal name of Israel's God. Rahab does not speak of a god in general. She names the God of these two strangers and says he is God over everything.

The word ‘kindness’ in verse 12 translates the Hebrew chesed. It means loyal love, the kind that keeps faith inside a relationship and goes beyond the least that is owed. It is the word the Old Testament uses most often for God's own love for Israel. Rahab has shown it to two foreigners at great risk. Now she asks to be shown it.

She does not ask for herself alone. She asks for her whole family, by name of kinship, down to ‘all who belong to them’.

An oath sworn in a god's name was the most binding promise the ancient world knew. The god was called on as witness and would hold the swearers to it. When the scouts say ‘our lives for your lives’, they are staking their own lives on keeping their word.
passages.later:
Israel had sung, on the far shore of the Red Sea, that this would happen. “The nations will hear and tremble” (Exodus 15:14), and ‘those who dwell in Canaan will melt away’ (Exodus 15:15).

The Old Testament says that a man named Salmon was the father of Boaz (Ruth 4:21). Matthew says who the mother was: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse” (Matthew 1:5). Jesse was the father of King David. Matthew sets all of this at the head of the family line of Jesus.
passages.asks: Everyone in Jericho heard the same reports. Only one household acted on them. Ask what you already know about God that you have not yet acted on. Then notice that Rahab asked for her whole family by name. Ask who you would name, and whether you have asked.

passages.happening:
Rahab's house was built into the city wall, so its window looked outside. She lets the two men down by a rope and gives them advice: “Go to the hill country,” she says, “so that your pursuers will not find you. Hide yourselves there for three days until they have returned; then go on your way” (verse 16).

Before they leave, the men set out the terms of the oath. She must tie a scarlet cord in the window they climbed out of. She must bring her whole family inside her house. Anyone who goes out into the street is responsible for his own death. Anyone harmed inside the house is the scouts' responsibility: ‘his blood will be on our heads’ (verse 19). And she must not tell anyone why they came.

“Let it be as you say,” she replies (verse 21). She sends them off and ties the cord in the window.

The men hide in the hills for three days, cross back over the river, and report to Joshua. Their report is Rahab's own words: “The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands,” they say. “Indeed, all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of us” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Fortified towns of that time often had houses built against the wall or inside it. Some cities had a double wall with rooms between the two faces, and people lived in them. A window in such a house opened to the outside of the city. That detail is why the escape was possible.

Rahab keeps thinking for the scouts. She knows the searchers have gone east toward the river, so she sends the men west into the hills and tells them how long to wait.

The men are careful about their oath because they mean to keep it. They say exactly what will bind them and what will release them. In a world where an oath called on God as witness, people did not swear loosely.

The cord is a sign for the day of the attack, so that the soldiers will know which house to leave alone. Some early Christian writers saw in its color a picture of the blood of Christ. The New Testament does not say that, and it is better held as a later devotional thought than as what the chapter means. The same Hebrew word can also mean ‘hope’, and readers should not build much on that either.

What the text does show is how quickly Rahab acts. The attack is still some way off. She ties the cord in the window as soon as the men are gone.

The scouts had been sent to look at the land. They come back with nothing about walls, gates or soldiers. They come back with what a Canaanite woman told them about the LORD, and that is the report Joshua hears.

One more thing is easy to miss. The law Israel carried said that the peoples of Canaan were to be given no treaty (Deuteronomy 7:2). The first thing Israel does in Canaan is swear to spare a Canaanite family. The book makes no comment on the tension. It tells the oath as kindness answered with kindness, and in chapter 6 it shows the oath kept.
passages.later:
The book returns to the house in the wall on the day Jericho falls. Joshua tells the two scouts, “Go into the house of the prostitute and bring out the woman and all who are with her, just as you promised her” (Joshua 6:22). And it gives the outcome: “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day” (Joshua 6:25).

The New Testament speaks of people who were once far from Israel's God and were brought near, as she was: “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).
passages.asks: Rahab tied the cord in the window the same hour, long before she needed it. Ask what small act of trust you keep putting off until the need is close. And think about her family, gathered in one house because one of them believed. Ask who is safer, or nearer to God, because of what you believe, and who might be if you spoke.
